events.description: Babbage completes the full design of the Analytical Engine
Prime Minister Peel reverses course and funds construction
Joseph Clement standardises the engine’s gears and screw threads
Ada Lovelace publishes Note G, the first program
The Engine computes Bernoulli numbers before the Royal Society
The Admiralty orders engines to compute navigation tables
Lloyd’s opens an actuarial engine room for the insurance market
The Bank of England moves its ledgers onto engines
Lovelace founds the School of Engine Programming in London
The 1851 census is tabulated entirely by engine
The Great Exhibition’s centrepiece is a working engine hall
Engines in London and Manchester exchange results by telegraph
Prussia buys three engines for its General Staff
Ten thousand clerks protest at Westminster against the engines
Manchester clerks hold a demonstration in solidarity
Parliament debates engine licensing legislation
Parliament passes the Engine Licensing Act
Moltke uses engine-planned railway timetables to mobilise
Britain and Prussia begin an engine arms race

arcs.name: Building the Engine
arcs.description: Babbage, Lovelace and Clement turn the design into working brass.

arcs.name: The Calculating Offices
arcs.description: Engines spread through the Admiralty, insurers and the census.

arcs.name: The Clerks’ Rebellion
arcs.description: Displaced clerks, rival powers and Parliament push back.

arcs.name: Engines on the Wire
arcs.description: Telegraphy links the engines into a network of tabulating houses.

relationships.evidence: The finished design made the cost estimate credible.
Funding paid for Clement’s workshop.
Standard parts made assembly possible.
Note G was written against the published design.
The demonstration ran Lovelace’s program.
Naval officers attended the demonstration.
Actuaries saw the tables could be trusted.
Demand for programmers outstripped Lovelace’s pupils.
The Register Office hired the first graduates.
Admiralty engines proved reliability at scale.
The census made the engine a national symbol.
Insurers wanted prices shared between cities.
Prussian officers toured the engine hall.
Census clerks were the first laid off.
Insurance clerks followed.
The Bank followed the insurers’ lead.
Word of the march reached Manchester by telegraph.
The march forced the question onto the Commons’ order paper.
The debate produced the Act.
The Act was Parliament’s answer to the march.
Networked engines made timetables tractable.
The General Staff’s engines planned the mobilisation.
Sadowa alarmed the Admiralty.
Licensing slowed British engines just as Prussia sped up.
